issues.explanation: Funerals/graves is hard to reconcile as a primary trigger for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision when the rest of the profile does not reference death-related loss, bereavement, or fatality cues; it stands apart from the other trigger and appraisal content in a way that is clinically difficult to explain.

Failed Role suggests a strong role-based or responsibility-based meaning of the trauma, but the rest of the profile does not indicate injury-related incapacity, inability to work, or family-protector themes that would support this appraisal. For this patient, it feels insufficiently grounded in the surrounding items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Permanent humiliation' is not impossible after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation and item set, which otherwise centers on fear-based post-collision threat, sensory reliving, and vulnerability rather than shame/humiliation. It is the least clinically integrated appraisal here and is hard to explain without other supporting shame-related items.

'Entrapment: Having no options' is not a clear contradiction, but for this trauma/profile it is weakly integrated compared with the other trigger items. The rest of the profile emphasizes crash reminders, reliving, danger appraisals, and hyperarousal. A strong entrapment trigger would usually be better supported by appraisals or memory content about being trapped or unable to escape, which are absent here.

vignette:
Six months ago, Robert was driving to an early-morning budget meeting at the high school where he had been principal for over a decade. He was approaching an intersection he had navigated perhaps ten thousand times before, thinking about the upcoming teacher evaluations, when a driver ran the red light. The impact tore through the driver's side door. Robert remembers the sound most of all - a deep, metallic roar folding into the shatter of glass - and then the crushing pressure of the airbag against his chest. He was extracted from the wreckage, hospitalized for a bruised sternum and a concussion, and told he was lucky. The other driver was fine. For the first few weeks, Robert told himself the same thing. He forced himself to focus solely on the positive narratives: he was alive, he was walking, he would return to work. He repeated this as though saying it forcefully enough could seal the crack he felt opening in his own mind.

By the second week at home, the crack had widened into a chasm. He began to replay the seconds before the collision obsessively, the film reversing and starting over before he could stop it. In these replays, he saw himself checking his blind spot more carefully, slowing down, avoiding the intersection altogether. A cruel certainty took root: somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. He began to feel that the crash had not been a random accident but a symptom of some fundamental failing in his own vigilance. The world outside his front door began to feel saturated with threat. Every car approaching an intersection was a potential missile. Every delay - a long traffic light, a stalled train on his commute - sent a surge of cold dread through his chest, a conviction that something terrible was unfolding just out of sight. He could not relax. Even in his living room, with the door locked, his body remained braced for impact.

Then came his first attempt to return to the school. He walked into the main office, and a student's mother in the waiting area began to shout at the secretary about a disciplinary issue. Robert froze. The raw, loud sound hit him like a physical blow, and the memory of the crash - the roar of metal - slammed into his present moment so vividly he could taste the dust from the airbag. He retreated into his office and closed the door, heart pounding, feeling the entire scene happening right now all over again. The building itself had become an engine of triggers. The clatter of lunch trays in the cafeteria was the sound of breaking glass. The loud cheer of a basketball game in the gym was a sonic assault. The drop-off line, where cars idled and bumped fenders, became a daily gauntlet of crash imagery. He found himself unable to put what he was feeling into words for his assistant principal or his wife. The experience was entirely sensory, a wash of pure terror that vanished the moment he opened his mouth to explain it.

To manage the overwhelming distress, Robert began to avoid the school altogether. First, he called in sick the days after the assembly. Then he took a formal medical leave of absence. The positive reframing he attempted - I just need rest, I will bounce back - rang hollow against the daily experience of his own mind. Sleep was a battleground; lying down meant being delivered directly back into the memory of the crash, a film that played on a loop until three in the morning, when he would finally give up and walk to the kitchen. There, he ate. He ate everything - leftovers, cereal, loaves of bread - a compulsive, mechanical attempt to fill the hollow dread that occupied his chest. His wife began to worry. She asked him to talk about it, but the words were not there. He told her he had permanently changed for the worse, that the old Robert - the decisive, steady leader his teachers relied on - was gone.

The school board has been calling, gently pressing for a return date. His assistant principal is struggling to hold the building together without him. Robert sits in my office, a large man who seems to be trying to fold into himself. He came not because he believes he can change, but because his wife asked, and because the absence from work is becoming a visible failure he cannot reframe. He is afraid of what he might find in therapy. He is deeply afraid of returning to the school, where he expects the loud noises and the shouting will put him right back in the driver's seat of that car. But he is even more afraid of what it means if he cannot go back. He wants to believe that therapy might help him find the version of himself he lost on that intersection, but deep down, he is certain the world is still a dangerous place, and that he is no longer equipped to lead anyone through it. That is where he begins.
